summary: Our project focuses on developing a smartwatch designed to monitor astronauts' health during long-duration space missions. Space travel exposes astronauts to challenges such as radiation, isolation, microgravity, bone density loss, and cardiovascular changes, which can affect their overall health and safety. Our proposed watch would track important health information, including heart rate, physical activity, sleep patterns, and other vital signs. This information could help astronauts and medical teams monitor changes in health, recognize potential concerns early, and make more informed decisions. By providing continuous and convenient health monitoring, the watch could reduce the need for constant manual checkups while keeping important health data accessible. This project is important because protecting astronauts' health is essential for the success of future space exploration missions, especially as humans travel farther from Earth and spend longer periods in space.
details:
Orbit Vitals is a 3D astronaut health monitoring app. It lets a crew member log their health data, see it on an interactive 3D human body, get alerts when something is off, and send reports to the medical team on Earth. Every reading is judged against NASA in-space reference ranges taken from published spaceflight research, not Earth norms. Where research shows no change in orbit, such as blood oxygen and respiratory rate, the app says so and uses the Earth range. It runs fully in the browser and keeps its data on the device.
The Home screen holds the astronaut's profile, including name, age, role, mission, medications with dose and frequency, and medical history. Below it are Organ Function Graphs, which are trend charts grouped by body system: heart, lungs and breathing, brain and behavior, kidneys and hydration, temperature and immune, bone and muscle, and stomach and nutrition. Each group shows a percentage of readings in range and a green healthy band, and you can touch a graph to read exact values. A reference table lists each indicator's in-space range beside its Earth range, with the research source and a short explanation.
The Body screen is a 3D human model you can rotate, zoom and tap. It includes the brain, heart, lungs, liver, stomach, kidneys and pancreas. Tapping an organ, or choosing it from the organ chips, opens a panel with that organ's current readings and an explanation of how it behaves in space, such as how heart output rises and blood pressure falls in orbit. A Focus organ button zooms in on the selected organ. A Health Analysis Report underneath gives a score for each organ system based on the latest readings.
The Log screen is where data goes in. An astronaut can enter heart rate, oxygen, blood pressure, respiration, temperature, sleep, mood, fatigue, stress, attention, exercise, grip strength, bone density, calcium, hydration, weight, nutrition, digestion, liver tests and ECG notes. Voice entry allows hands-free logging, and a voice check-up can read replies aloud. Recent entries are listed below, and one button loads 14 days of demo data so every feature can be seen working.
The Alerts screen warns when readings leave the in-space range and gives a recommendation. It compares readings with the astronaut's own baseline, records symptoms or eye issues with severity and the response taken, and queues serious alerts for the medical crew on Earth with a simulated communication delay. The link to Earth is simulated for the demo.
The Watch screen pairs over Bluetooth with heart-rate watches, chest straps and armbands, and shows live heart rate, SpO₂ and HRV on a moving graph. A simulator covers devices without Bluetooth support. Workout mode adds a timer, heart-rate zones, average and maximum heart rate, and a saved workout history.
The Coach screen is a Mission Coach chat that answers questions about sleep, heart rate, oxygen, exercise, hydration, mood and blood pressure using the astronaut's own logged data, with one-tap prompts like "Summarize my week". It gives general wellness guidance only and sends clinical concerns to the flight surgeon.
The Crew screen compares several astronauts, lets you switch between them, and adds a cabin environment log for CO₂, temperature and humidity. The Game screen, called the Mission Health Race, is a 3D scene with daily quests, XP, levels, badges and standings. A player's race score combines routine points for check-ups, sleep, exercise, hydration and nutrition with the percentage of their vitals inside NASA in-space ranges. The Reports screen generates a total health report for each astronaut that bundles readings, alerts, symptoms, medications, history, workouts and routine. Reports are saved on the device, open offline, and are logged when sent to Earth.
Orbit Vitals puts an astronaut's whole health picture in one place instead of scattered logs, watches and notes. Because readings are judged against in-space ranges, a value that looks abnormal on Earth but is normal in orbit, such as lower blood pressure, does not trigger a false alarm. Comparing readings with the astronaut's own baseline helps catch slow changes early. Hands-free voice logging helps when a crew member is busy or wearing gloves. Offline reports mean health records are available even when the connection to Earth is lost. Encrypted local storage keeps sensitive health data private. The health race game motivates astronauts to keep up healthy routines such as sleep, hydration and exercise over a long mission.
The goal is to help crews on long-duration missions look after their own health when a hospital is far away and communication with Earth is delayed. By turning raw numbers into clear scores, alerts and a body they can explore, Orbit Vitals aims to help astronauts and flight surgeons notice problems sooner and act on them. The same approach could also support people in other remote and isolated places, such as polar stations, submarines and rural clinics.
Orbit Vitals is built with HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript as a single web page. The 3D body and race scene use Three.js, with custom GLSL shaders for the glowing organ and body effects, and the health graphs are drawn on the HTML Canvas. Live vitals use the Web Bluetooth API, voice entry and spoken replies use the Web Speech API, and the optional PIN lock uses the Web Crypto API (AES-GCM encryption). Data is stored in the browser's local storage, and the interface uses the Manrope typeface. The Mission Coach is built to use an AI assistant and falls back to a built-in rules-based coach when AI is not available. No special hardware is needed: it runs on any modern device with a browser, and it can optionally connect to Bluetooth heart-rate watches, chest straps and armbands.
Instead of tables of numbers, Orbit Vitals gives astronauts a glowing 3D body they can rotate and tap to explore each organ in an in-space context. It treats health tracking as a mission by adding quests, levels, badges and a crew race, tied to real NASA in-space ranges. It joins voice logging, wearable sensors, Earth alert queuing, offline reports and encryption in a single app, in a futuristic purple mission-control style with a light and dark theme.
We considered that normal values in space differ from those on Earth, so every range is based on published research and sourced in the app. We designed for the conditions of a mission: limited connectivity, so the app works offline; privacy, so data stays on the device with optional encryption; and busy crews, so voice entry and a mobile-first layout are included. We considered safety, so the coach gives general wellness guidance only and sends clinical concerns to the flight surgeon. We also considered device support, so a simulator covers browsers without Bluetooth, and we made clear that the link to Earth is simulated for the demo.
